t: Why You Must Forgive Misbehaving Students

t: Five Men of Character Who Shaped History
q: In our modern times, popular culture tends to celebrate image and self-expression. For this reason one might assume that greatness is about doing what is best for oneself. However, if we step back and study the great men in history, we will get a different idea of greatness.

Marcus Aurelius ruled the Roman Empire during one of its most turbulent periods. His time was marked by foreign wars, internal instability, and a devastating plague. Although he held absolute power, he regarded his authority as a burden that demanded character and restraint.

William Wilberforce moved easily within Britain's political and social elite. After a profound moral awakening, he dedicated his life to ending the British slave trade. For more than forty years, Wilberforce faced ridicule and fierce opposition.

While some men would have crumbled, Shackleton devoted himself entirely to his men by maintaining morale and enforcing discipline. Against the odds, he did not lose a single man on the journey and all were rescued.

The men who shaped our world were often those who accepted responsibility willingly and served others before themselves. Character is not a relic of the past. It is the foundation of anything worth building and preserving.” Archived from The Ways of a Gentleman (Martin Substack) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.

t: From Disparate Knowledge to Unified Fluency Freedom: Generalising the Ratio Table (Part 1)
q: [1] "Unit conversion, similar shapes, scale factors, scale diagrams. In your classroom, do your students see these as a unified set of proportional concepts, or do they hold disparate knowledge? I think too often, the answer is the latter.

[2] "The true test of the ratio table scaffold is its ability to generalise. Does the ratio table only work for simple linear conversions? Or can it successfully manage the complexities of area, volume, and beyond to other work such as similar shapes? So do they generalise, yes they do!
[3] "Because the conversion factor applies to both the length and the width, we must square the underlying linear relationship. The Ratio Table makes this connection explicit and transparent.

[4] "We now see that 1 m 2 = 10,000 cm 2 . This is no longer only a fact to be memorised; it is a relationship derived from the known linear fact. Is it bad to memorise facts? No, but if we have connected knowledge we are more likely to be able to use that knowledge, or fall back to the connection if the factual knowledge starts to fade.

[5] "Volume is measured in cubic units (L 3 ). Following the same logic, if the conversion factor applies across all three dimensions (length, width, and height), we must cube the underlying linear ratio.

[6] "The Ratio Table is not just an alternative method for unit conversion; it is a mathematical framework that reveals the underlying proportional structure across different contexts... This is a consistent, non-negotiable mathematical truth, derived directly from the dimension of the measure.

[7] "By grounding both metric unit conversions and the scale factors for similar shapes in the same principle (the relationship between L, L 2 , and L 3 ), we give our students a single, powerful model to generalise across traditionally separate topics. We replace rote memorisation with structural understanding.

q: Their findings suggest that spaced practice generally enhances mathematics retention, with a more pronounced effect for isolated concepts versus material embedded in a course.

Teachers should primarily focus on spacing out mathematics practice over multiple sessions rather than concentrating it into a single massed session.
Many mathematics textbooks are structured in a massed manner, presenting all questions on a topic immediately after it's learned.
In classroom settings, it's often unclear if students genuinely retrieve information or simply rely on accessible notes, potentially diminishing the effect.

t: Expertise: The Best Professional Investment You Can Make

t: Why Do I Need to Know This
q: New knowledge is like a ratchet: once knowledge and skills are securely stored in long-term memory, they don't just sit there—they make the next layer of learning possible. Each new concept builds on what came before, allowing students to handle ideas that would have been impossible or overwhelmingly difficult a few years earlier.

We teach the multiplication tables not because adults need to multiply numbers by hand, but because they are a gateway concept. Automaticity in basic operations frees up working memory, which in turn facilitates the learning of fractions, ratios, proportional reasoning, algebra, and much of higher mathematics.

Learning can be likened to the construction of a multi-storey building. For weeks, all that seems to happen is digging, pouring concrete, laying rebar, and checking measurements. To an outside observer—especially one who doesn't understand construction—it can look as though nothing useful is being built. But the crew is constructing the foundation that will support everything that comes later.

When students ask, 'Why do we need to know this?', they are often not asking a philosophical question about curriculum design. More often, it is a sign they are experiencing confusion, fatigue, or frustration. In those moments, a speech about relevance misses the point.

A student who understands what is going on is less likely to wonder why the content matters. When students experience clarity, progress, and competence, effort begins to feel worthwhile. They feel a sense of accomplishment and can appreciate their new understanding.” Archived from Science of Learning Substack on April 21, 2026 by Tim.

t: Spiral Dynamics: The Hidden Patterns That Shape Your Team's Behavior
q: Not everyone sees the world the same way. Not everyone is driven by growth, or impact, or freedom. Some people want structure. Others want meaning. Some just want stability. So, what you're really facing is a values mismatch, not a motivation problem.

Spiral Dynamics is a model that helps you understand the underlying values that drive people, and how those values evolve over time. At its core, Spiral Dynamics says this: People (and teams) operate from different value systems. These value systems shape how they think, what they care about, and how they respond to leadership.

If someone on your team is in the 'stability and safety' mode, and you start talking to them about 'growth and purpose', you're likely to lose them. Spiral Dynamics gives you a way to see that mismatch, and fix it.

What makes Spiral Dynamics powerful is that it helps you see the invisible: the underlying logic behind someone's choices, motivations, and resistance. What I like most about this model is that it turns culture from something fuzzy and abstract into something you can observe, name, and work with.

Without it, you're guessing. With it, you're leading with confidence and precision. And once you see your team through this lens, you'll start to notice things you missed before: the invisible patterns that shape your culture, your team dynamics, and even your biggest challenges.” Archived from The Good Boss Substack on April 21, 2026 by Tim.

t: Research Bite #52: Three Types of Conceptual Change: Belief Revision, Mental Model Transformation, and Categorical Shift
q: The provided text explores three distinct types of conceptual change in learning, particularly within science education: belief revision, mental model transformation, and categorical shift. It distinguishes between learning that simply adds or completes prior knowledge and the more complex process of changing existing, incorrect ideas.
The author argues that false beliefs can be revised through direct refutation, and flawed mental models can be transformed by accumulating multiple belief revisions.

The text emphasizes that robust misconceptions, often found in scientific domains, necessitate a more profound categorical shift, where a concept is reclassified into a different lateral or ontological category due to a fundamental misunderstanding of its nature.
This deeper form of conceptual change requires learners to be aware of their category mistake and to build a new, appropriate category for understanding.

For robust misconceptions, teachers should understand they often stem from category mistakes, not just false beliefs. Refuting individual beliefs is often insufficient. Instead, instruction must aim for categorical shifts by making students aware of these fundamental errors and building new, appropriate categories.

If you're a funny person, you can use this study as a guideline. Don't mock your students; you knew that anyway. Don't waste time with jokes about Saturday Night Live; they're not having the effect you hope they do.

t: Research Bite #51: A Cornerstone of Adaptivity -- A Meta-Analysis of the Expertise Reversal Effect
q: This article presents a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect (ERE), a phenomenon where instructional assistance benefits novices but hinders experts. The researchers conducted a systematic literature search, including 60 experimental studies with 5924 participants, to evaluate the ERE's strength and identify moderators.

Their findings confirm that low-knowledge learners benefit significantly from high assistance, while high-knowledge learners perform better with low assistance. The study also highlights that the ERE is asymmetrical, with providing assistance to novices having a stronger positive impact than withholding it from experts.
Educational status and content domain were found to moderate these effects, suggesting varied applicability across different learning contexts and age groups.

If teachers remember one thing, it should be to adjust instructional methods based on learners' domain knowledge. Novices benefit significantly from high assistance, while experts learn better with low assistance. Critically, providing assistance to novices has a stronger beneficial impact than withholding it from experts, so when in doubt, it's better to provide assistance.

Utilise tools for adaptation: Intelligent tutoring systems are a promising option for designing instruction aligned with the Expertise Reversal Effect, as they can track and adapt to learner knowledge levels in real time.

t: You Should Use Mini Whiteboards
q: This is the absolute best way to check for understanding. In very little time, I can sample the entire class and get a sense of what students know and don't know. Mini whiteboards are a bit slow: I ask a question, then I wait until every student has a chance to answer, then students hold their boards up, then I take a moment to scan, and then we are on to the next question.

So here's the routine: students write their answer to a question, then they 'flip and hover': they flip the whiteboard upside down and hold it hovering above the desk. This serves two purposes: one, it reduces cheating, and two, it signals for you which students are finished.
In all of this I have to distinguish between students who are confused, and students who are opting out. If a student is confused, I offer them support and make sure it isn't framed as a punishment.
This felt really hard. And in the long term, this type of checking for understanding drove a ton of positive changes in my teaching.

It cannot anticipate where the next fire will be, so it has to shape an energetic and efficient team that is capable of responding to the unanticipated as well as to any ordinary event. (Andrew Grove)
Spend zero time on what you could have done, and devote all of your time on what you might do. (Ben Horowitz)” Archived from The Business Leader Daily Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: What Is the Most Human Aspect of Leadership
q: Leadership is a human concept and we all iterate on our own personal view of being a leader. So by default does that mean any and all aspects of leadership, in all its forms are human? I would argue no.

You don't need to dig too deeply into recent headlines to see examples of dehumanizing and downright evil leaders. Manipulating, cajoling and other means of reaching a goal are human behaviors but do they add or subtract from everyone's lived experience.
That is the key here. Good leaders add to the work environment and/or home. Takers subtract.
For me, the most human aspects of leadership include connection and trust but there are more aspects to be considered. Empathy, Authenticity, Inclusivity, Humor, Culture, Safety.
Be kind to yourself but grade yourself honestly. For example, am I being authentic at work or am I pretending to be someone I am not?

Take the knowledge you glean from the introspection seek ways to improve and grow. Sometimes it might be as simple as remembering to smile more. While other topics might lead you to read articles about aligning actions with your values.” Archived from The Inner Call (Tim Draayer Substack) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: What Actually Works in Instructional Coaching
q: The 'Thinking Out Loud' episodes on Better Teaching: Only Stuff That Works are a running set of conversations to make sense of instruction, coaching, and implementation as they actually function in schools — not as we wish they did.

The premise is straightforward: Gene Tavernetti and I take a concrete problem of practice, name what tends to go wrong, and work toward clearer thinking and more usable actions for teachers, coaches, and leaders.

We dig into rehearsal as a missing 'bridge' between professional development and actual classroom change. If teachers only talk about strategies (or just watch someone else do them), transfer is shaky. Rehearsal, paired with feedback, helps convert ideas into actions teachers can reliably pull off with students.

We zoom in on what coaches actually do during observations. Observation isn't passive — what you attend to, how you collect evidence, and how you frame what you saw all shape whether the debrief becomes helpful (or demoralizing).

We take on a classic staffing dilemma: pulling great teachers out of classrooms can hurt students, but schools also need credible, skilled coaches. We talk through the opportunity costs, why great teaching doesn't automatically equal great coaching.

Here I reflect on what consulting teaches you about implementation and change: what leaders think they want vs. what will actually move practice, why 'big splash' training often fades, and why alignment and follow-through matter more than inspiration.” Archived from Education Rickshaw on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: Theyve Always Been This Way So Get Ready
q: They blew past their curfew, again. They woke up grouchy, again. They ignored you and walked away in the middle of a conversation. They are convinced the world revolves around them. They think they know better about everything.

I have tried to make sure that a reader can feel inside the characters in the poem, to convey the ways that each character in the poem has her or his own distinctive point of view, the immaturity and vulnerability of Telemachus, for example, when he tries to speak out against the suitors, but ends up bursting into tears.

Some of the other words she translated for 'immature' Telemachus across the epic poem: Moodily. Brooding. Sullen. Sound familiar? That's every teenager ever. That was you. That is (or is going to be) your kid. That was every kid in ancient Greece, too.

Kids are kids. Always have been and always will be. Teenagers will do teenage things and have teenage attitudes. That's how it goes. It shouldn't surprise us. It shouldn't be taken personally, only prepared for.
If anything, it should be appreciated, because it's a tradition, apparently an ancient one, for them to be this way.” Archived from The Daily Dad on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Real Learning Value of Kids Playing Many Kinds of Games
q: When adults talk about kids and games, the conversation usually collapses into a single question: 'But what are they learning?' It sounds reasonable. But it misses where the real learning is happening. Because games don't primarily teach content. They train the systems that make learning possible in the first place.

When kids rotate games, strategy games, physical games, cooperative games, imaginative games, or play games that have a lot of moving parts, they're doing something cognitively powerful without knowing the term for it. They're interleaving.
All the different rules, social dynamics, strategies and challenges/fails/iterations create friction, meaning more mental effort. That friction matters because it is what helps kids learn faster.

You can explain executive function skills to kids: planning, focus, working memory, flexible thinking, resilience. But explanation doesn't equal ownership. Kids who learn EF through play learn it by doing, which means they own those skills.
Kids don't have weak executive function because they lack explanations. They have weak EF because they don't get enough real-life practice.

When a game starts feeling like school — when the outcome is predetermined and there's no room to iterate and discover a unique experience or solution — kids' intrinsic motivation crashes. Kids zone out.

The question isn't: 'Is this game educational?' It's: 'What exploration (read executive demands) does this game offer my child, and how much room does it leave for unique solutions?'” Archived from Quest for Learning (Shari Keller Substack) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Problem with Your New Years Resolution
q: It's the second week of 2026. Have you kept your New Year's resolution? For many, the answer is probably no. Perhaps you are reading this sentence while, filled with self-loathing, you eat something you vowed to forgo in 2026.
Of about half of all Americans who make New Year's resolutions on January 1, 22 percent have failed at the end of week one; 50 percent at three months; and 81 percent after two years.

Knowing this, you might conclude that New Year's resolutions are stupid. That would be a mistake. Resolutions are very good, in fact: They are a sign that you want to improve your life in tangible ways, which is healthy and positive. People need something in their lives that's worth striving for.

I used to wake up each night around 3 a.m. and light up a coffin nail right there in the bed. But one night at age 26, when I was engaged to be married, I fell back asleep with a lit cigarette, and woke up later with 10 holes burned in the sheets.
It occurred to me that it was one thing for the cigs to kill me, but quite another for them to kill the future Mrs. Brooks.
You just have to be smart about how to make your resolutions.” Archived from The Free Press (The Pursuit of Happiness with Arthur Brooks) on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Leadership Skill of Anticipating Resistance
q: Most resistance or controversy can be predicted and offset before it appears.
The skill of anticipating resistance is largely one of audience interpretation.

Asking What is the worst or most negative interpretation the primary audience could make of this decision, action, or message narrows the list of reasons and gives leaders insight into where resistance is likely to show itself.
The strongest leaders aren’t surprised by resistance or controversy.
Smart leaders know resistance is always the biggest obstacle they face.

t: Servant Leadership How to Lead Better by Getting Out of the Way
q: Most leadership advice is about being in the spotlight. You're told to own the room, set the vision, and drive results. You get praised for being in control, for being 'the expert', for always having the answers.
But what if that leadership advice is completely wrong? What if the best leaders don't take the spotlight, but instead… step back?
Servant Leadership flips the most fundamental element of leadership. Instead of asking, 'How can my team help me succeed?', a servant leader asks, 'How can I help my team succeed?'

Servant Leadership doesn't mean you do everyone's job. It doesn't mean you avoid hard decisions. It means your primary role as a leader is to build people. Their growth becomes your success. Their wins become your scoreboard.

Most managers default to control, and most leadership models work top-down. The leader sits at the top of the pyramid, followed by management, then employees, with the customer at the very bottom. Instructions, pressure, and decisions flow downward.

Servant leadership flips that pyramid. At the bottom is the leader, and at the very top is the customer. Instead of control flowing down, support flows up. Your job as a leader is no longer to command. It's to serve: to remove blockers, grow people, and create an environment where your team can succeed.” Archived from The Good Boss Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: Research Bite #50: The Five-Year Itch: Motivational Factors That Influence the Career Decisions of Early Career Teachers in England
q: This academic article explores the motivational factors influencing early career teachers' (ECTs) decisions to stay or leave the profession in England. The study identifies key push and pull factors, such as the increasing complexity and relentlessness of the role, its emotional impact, alongside the profound sense of belonging and the development of a positive professional identity.

Teachers should remember that fostering a positive professional identity and cultivating meaningful relationships within the school community and with students are crucial. This autonomous motivation significantly reduces intentions to quit, supporting well-being and retention, especially in the first five years of their careers.

The study included 20 Early Career Teachers (ECTs) from state-funded primary, secondary, and special schools in England. All participants had less than 5 years' teaching experience. The group was diverse in age and gender, largely reflecting the demographics of teachers in England.

This paper uniquely applies Self-Determination Theory to explore the motivational needs and perspectives of Early Career Teachers (ECTs), an area previously underexplored. It identifies specific push and pull factors influencing their career decisions, highlighting that autonomous motivation reduces quitting intentions.

The increasing complexity of the teaching role impacts classroom practice by creating additional non-student-facing administrative duties. This can hinder teachers' ability to focus on student interaction and their core teaching responsibilities.

For example, managing the increasing number of students with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) adds to the administrative burden, potentially taking time away from direct teaching and support within the classroom. Teachers may feel ill-equipped to handle the multifaceted needs of students, leading to anxiety and low self-efficacy in the classroom.

t: How Leaders Destroy Their Best Teams
q: When it comes to creating a high-performing team, there's one trait that matters more than any other. It's not individual talent. It's not accountability. It's also not structure or hierarchy or even the team members being friends. The single most important element to successfully creating a high-performing team is… Psychological safety.

The number one predictor of successful teams is whether or not people feel safe speaking up. Teams perform better when people feel safe to make mistakes, challenge ideas, and disagree without fear. That's psychological safety.
Leaders don't ignore psychological safety because they think it doesn't matter. They ignore it because it makes them feel less in control. When it comes right down to it, control is about ego.
Psychological safety is created or destroyed by the leaders behavior. Period. Full stop. If you're the leader, you are fully responsible for psychological safety.

When no one pushes back on your ideas… When meetings don't address the tension… When most decisions seem to be unanimous… Some leaders call that alignment. But they're wrong. When there is no pushback, there is usually no psychological safety.

Maintaining high standards is really important for maintaining psychological safety. After all you can't have a high-performing team without high standards. The safest teams are the ones that argue and debate and disagree, and they can do it all without fear of retaliation or being berated.
You don't destroy psychological safety with your policies. You destroy it with your behavior.” Archived from The Best Leadership Newsletter on May 1, 2026 by Tim.

t: A Year of The Fatherhood Framework
q: Hard as it is for me to believe, it has now been a full year since I published the first Fatherhood Framework post.

I have been struck by how much parents actually agree on, even when their politics look nothing alike. Most want families to stand on firmer ground, without feeling like every decision is a financial or logistical gamble.
Not outright hostility toward parenting per se, but indifference to it. Indifference to kids. Indifference to families. Indifference to whether public policy is designed with parents in mind at all.
The long-standing tension between parent voters and retiree voters is shifting again, as a growing share of the population has no direct stake in family policy and little interest in defending it.

The math is simple. You cannot sustain social systems without future generations. You cannot have future generations without children. And you cannot expect people to choose to have children without an environment that treats parenting as a priority.
Everything I write is made with you in mind. This project is my gift to you.” Archived from Fatherhood Framework Substack on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Why Debate Becomes Critical Infrastructure in the Singularity
q: The crisis is not that machines become intelligent. It is that human judgment atrophies while machine output proliferates.

By the time anyone notices, the infrastructure for human judgment has atrophied. People still vote, approve policies, make decisions. But the real choices have already been made.
Debate is how humans rehearse staying in charge of choices that matter.

That institutional skepticism creates a firewall against automated authority and preserves human judgment as the ultimate check on machine optimization.” Archived from Stefan Bauschard Substack on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The choreography of teaching 30 children at the same time
q: In my opinion the practicalities - the mechanics, the routines - of running a room so that every single individual in it is learning, are not sufficiently examined and spelt out in our training and professional discourse.
How will I make sure EVERYONE is learning? [The key question underlying all choreography decisions]

Students do not learn simply by being in a room where other people are learning. They each need to be active participants and, if we want to ensure learning is happening, we need to check that it is – for everyone.

The key is to engineer full attention intentionally, not assume it. It's natural and inevitable that students – with their pesky human brains – will mind-wander unless they have a strong pull to concentrate.

t: The Basics Abandonment Problem

t: How to Get Your Students' Silent Attention Anytime You Want

t: Rethinking Fast and Slow
q: If intuition, properly structured, can reliably produce correct answers without deliberation, then the goal of education cannot simply be to teach students to think more slowly and carefully.

t: From distress to eustress: why some stress is good for you
q: Eustress is the productive strain that accompanies deliberate practice. The feeling students get when they are required to retrieve information rather than recognise it, to explain ideas rather than copy them.
The relationship between arousal and performance follows an inverted U-shaped curve. Too little pressure produces apathy and superficial engagement. Too much overwhelms attention and working memory.
Learning happens most reliably in the uncomfortable middle, where effort is required but success still feels attainable.
That cognitive demand is precisely what strengthens memory and understanding.

We are prone to treating stress as an educational toxin, something to be eliminated wherever possible. Yet the evidence suggests something more nuanced.” Archived from David Didau Substack on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Visualisers: The Classroom Tool I Can't Teach Without
q: I've even been in classrooms where the visualiser is plugged in but abandoned on the floor, buried under books. Not because teachers don't want to use it—because no one has shown them how. And that's not their fault.
Visualisers help us manage that load. They take unnecessary thinking away — Where do I write this? How should it look? Which bit goes here? — so pupils can focus on the actual learning.
You model a written addition on a big piece of flip chart paper. You remind them: neat layout, one digit per box, line up the digits. They start work.
You model the calculation under your visualiser using your own teacher model book. You show one digit per box, lay out the next calculation underneath, explain your thinking aloud. They start work.
Now you can live mark effectively. You can see misconceptions easily. Children can self-check. You're not repeating yourself.

Children can share their writing by placing their book under the visualiser. Their classmates can follow the text, celebrate success, and support editing. This kind of modelling is powerful because the class can see real writing, in a real book, in real time.

t: Tune Into the Five Lead Indicators of Team Health

t: Regularities, All the Way Down
q: But underneath the friction, Kris was trying to argue that cognitive scientists give us theories of learning, but not theories of instruction. They tell us how the brain processes information, but they don't tell us what to say to a room of thirty 14-year-olds on a Tuesday morning.

It is extraordinarily tempting to believe that the higher layers will ultimately make the lower ones unnecessary. There are good reasons for this temptation. One is intellectual: human beings are pattern-hungry.

t: Questioning Coaching 2026

t: Why New Year Resolutions Fail Without Character We are one week into the New Year and most of us are probably sticking to our resolutions
q: We are one week into the New Year and most of us are probably sticking to our resolutions. By February, the number will have dropped dramatically.

A resolution to exercise, eat healthily, or read more requires discipline, persistence, and the ability to delay gratification—all character traits.

t: When Emotions Run Too High in the Workplace

Insist on holding the value of respect higher than the value of self-expression.

t: The Trap of Teaching "Hacks": Why Shortcuts Are Not Solutions

t: Are You an Independent Thinker

t: A Simple "Experience Sampling" Method for Making Big Decisions About Your Career or Your Life our-career-or-your-life

For the next 10 days, set some alarms in your phone: one before school starts, one during lunch or on prep, one sometime after school is done. When the alarm goes off, grab your notebook and jot your first-response answers to a few questions

t: What I Got Wrong About Leadership

t: The Greatest Shortcut for Leaders Is Reading Books

Being busy at work or at home isn't a good reason not to read. It's an argument for why you should.
The Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius prized the ability to read attentively, mostly philosophy texts, and used what he learned to reign masterfully over his domain.

No one gets anywhere in this world in any really and endurable manner without some recourse to books. Reading is also a shortcut, a way to get where you want to get without having to learn by painful trial and error.” Archived from Daily Stoic on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Ontario Has a Math Emergency
q: Students cannot reason effectively about ideas they have not yet learned. Working memory is limited. Without clear explanations, modelling and guided practice, even capable learners become overwhelmed.
Knowledge frees up thinking. Fluency makes problem-solving possible. Crucially, explicit instruction benefits the students who struggle the most.

We would never hand a child a flute and ask them to discover how to play before teaching notes and scales. Nor would we start swim lessons in the deep end. Yet in math, we often reverse this sequence.

Countries with high-performing education systems, such as Singapore, Japan and Estonia, have long built their math programs on these principles. Britain has recently moved in the same direction, with measurable gains.

If Ontario wants better outcomes, three actions are clearly needed: strengthen teacher education in evidence-based math instruction; adopt curriculum materials that guide teachers toward clarity rather than guesswork; and build foundational fluency with math facts early and explicitly.” Archived from Science of Learning on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Long Days, Short Years
q: Eighteen years sounds like a long time. It isn't. All of it felt slow while it was happening. None of it feels slow now.
The days are long, but the years are short. From learning to walk through graduation, the blur of childhood passes faster than expected.
I know you're tired. I know you feel like you're failing some days. I know you feel overwhelmed. But the golden years usually don't look golden while you're in them.
Embrace it. It's short. It's unique. It doesn't come back.

For parents in the thick of childhood chaos, embracing the unique, unrepeatable season matters more than waiting for clarity that comes only after it ends.” Archived from This Is Foster on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Happiness Lessons from a Miserable Wretch
q: I am a specialist in the science of human happiness. Just as a professional athlete must be naturally athletic, you might think I am a naturally happy person. I'm not.
The mind-made nature of our mass misery means there is enormous demand for something better, a cultural renaissance of love, meaning, and spiritual nutrition.
Getting happier is a skill like any other. You need to understand the science, change your habits and behavior in tangible ways, and explain what you have learned to others.
For the first time in my life, I feel I have a sacred vocation: to lift others up and bring them together. Life feels richer than it ever did, more alive, more full of love.

The freedom to pursue happiness is the secret to building a truly great nation, one that is a gift to civilization. It isn't easy, but it is one of the most worthwhile pursuits in the world.” Archived from The Free Press on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Do You Project the Identity You Want To
q: The identity a leader projects influences how people respond to them.
Decide exactly what is most important for you to be seen as.
Don’t confuse what you value and what identity you want others to conclude about you.
Just because you value and believe you are compassionate doesn’t mean you act compassionately in the eyes of others.
The good news is that no one can project a false image over time.
Remember, people will respond and engage based upon who they see you to be, not who you believe you are.

t: Agency Is the Oxygen of Learning
q: Kids care most about the work they take part in, not the work they just carry out. When your kid has no role in their own learning, they don't have a role in thinking.
When kids lose ownership of the micro decisions inside thinking, nothing dramatic happens. But your kid stops thinking for themselves. They're finishing a task, not working with it.

The safest approach becomes something like: Just tell me what you want, and I'll do that. Sure it might produce a good student who gets good grades but your kid's willingness to bring their own ideas usually drops off.

Kids don't really learn just by carrying out instructions. They learn when they think. All those micro moments when your kid tries first, even before they fully understand, is the oxygen that fuels learning.

Restoring ownership doesn't mean pulling away. It means inviting your kid back into the thinking in small ways, consistently and with compassion, as a coach who believes your kid can do it.” Archived from Quest for Learning on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Student Voice is Shocking
q: I guarantee that you will report much higher, not slightly higher, scores than the national average.
Ask your own students, use the scores to celebrate where you are better than national, use the scores to work out how to improve the experience of your students.
The national results are shocking and should concern every school leader.
Student voice data provides a crucial diagnostic tool for school improvement efforts.
Schools that regularly monitor student voice can identify and address engagement gaps systematically.” Archived from Dominic's School Improvement Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Questioning Coaching
q: The relationship between coach and coachee is central to success in instructional coaching.
Many schools have not adequately thought through the two-tiered system they are creating when implementing coaching.
What passes for instructional coaching varies wildly from program to program across the country.
The effectiveness of coaching depends greatly on the expertise level of the teacher being coached.
Schools need to be honest about whether instructional coaching actually fits their cultural and structural context.” Archived from Carousel Teaching on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: How to Create More Commitment to Decisions and Tasks
q: When team members are committed to a decision or task, they become energized and invested.
The first idea to keep in mind is that people increase their commitment after they start moving.
The more public the commitment, the more ownership people feel for the process and the outcome.
When team members connect the dots and see that vision and values depend upon execution, they identify with it deeply.

The deepest commitment is always one where a team member sees themselves holding hands with the organization's vision and values through their actions.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Don't Forget to Elaborate
q: Elaboration simply means adding something to information you've absorbed. That could consist of making a connection between different texts or between a text and a student's pre-existing knowledge or opinions.
We want students to engage in deep, meaningful, thoughtful processing. And that is what we really mean when we're talking about elaboration.
Only the two groups who engaged in elaboration—by coming up with their own examples—achieved deeper comprehension.
Elaborative activities are what all students need to realize their full academic and cognitive potential.

One relatively simple way to ensure that students are engaging in both retrieval practice and elaboration is to have teachers embed a coherent method of writing instruction in whatever content they're teaching.” Archived from Minding the Gap on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Why Your Students Don't Like You; And What To Do About It
q: All students want to like their teacher. But most of them don't.
The main reason students don't like their teachers is not because teachers have something wrong with them personally.
Students are drawn to teachers who create a sense of safety and fairness in the classroom environment.
The foundation of good relationships between teachers and students is reliability and consistency.
Students respect and like teachers who care genuinely about their growth and wellbeing as whole people.” Archived from Smart Classroom Management on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: This Job Is Killing Me
q: Working 55 hours or more per week is a serious health hazard with documented negative health outcomes.
Reducing hours, say, from 55 to 50 hours a week, would have had only small effects on output.
More is caught than taught. Leading by example is one of the first laws of leadership.
The wealthiest 10% often work the most because working long hours symbolizes wealth and importance in their minds.
Workaholism has become like a new religion, and leaders must actively work against this cultural norm.” Archived from Lead You First on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Nehemiah's Secret to Completing Goals
q: People simply do not know how to properly set and pursue goals with the discipline and purpose they require.
With purpose, discipline comes easier, because you will have an answer to the pestering question that bothers everyone.
Most people's resolutions lack a solid foundation in the form of a deeper purpose worth suffering for.
If God puts a purpose in your heart, it's cowardly, prideful, and irresponsible not to pursue it.
Deep purpose grounded in pain and desire to save others from it is where worthy goals begin.” Archived from Simple Men on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Identifying the Levels of Team Member Commitment
q: Contrary to what many team leaders believe, team member commitment is not binary.
Understanding that commitment exists along a continuum is essential for creating more of it.
This is why leadership experts often claim that consensus is less important than commitment.
This ownership matters a great deal. A decision everyone agrees with, but no one feels responsible for, often fails.
This higher level of commitment exists when team members come to believe the decision or task is connected to their values and self-identity.
A concentrated strength of high commitment outperforms an evenness of moderate devotion nearly every time.

t: Make Yourself More Interesting in the New Year
q: People move toward those they find more interesting, and they present those folks with opportunities often denied to others whom they find more commonplace.
Interest in others is about what you give, no matter how exciting they seem.
But what makes people interesting over the long term is not what they do or have done, but in how they think.
We are most drawn to people who think differently than others.
Generating unique views is not as hard as many believe, although it does take time, deep reflection, and a creative openness to see things others don’t.
How interesting are you? Make it a point to become more interesting this year.
